note: Extracted 14 September 2026 from permissively licensed reviews (CC BY, or public domain for the 1998 US government overview), each licence read in the retrieved full text, with no text-and-data-mining or AI restriction found. OpenStax is excluded (D-26). Elphick et al. 2018 was not used: it carries a published correction whose text could not be obtained. Every quote was checked word for word against the retrieved text. Endogenous examples are the sources' own; none is a statement about treatment.

topic.title: Peptides the body makes
topic.publicationChapter: Understanding Peptides — Three: Peptides in the human body
topic.summary: What reviews of physiology say about the body's own peptides: the classes they fall into, how they are made from larger precursors, stored and released, how they are broken down, and why what a peptide does depends on context. General biology, not statements about any peptide product.
topic.notes: Growth factors as a class, a general statement that the body's peptides are short-lived, and the inference that 'the body makes it' is not an argument about safety or efficacy are not stated by any source held, and are recorded as gaps.

claims.claimText: Hevesi, Hökfelt and Harkany (2025) describe the classical view that neuropeptides are made as long prepropeptides, processed by enzymes into active peptides, stored in large dense-core vesicles and released in an activity-dependent way.
claims.plainLanguageText: Neuropeptides are first made as longer chains. Enzymes trim them into their active form, and they are stored until the nerve cell is active enough to release them.
claims.interpretationNotes: Authors label this "classical concepts" and note newer findings (dendritic release, local synthesis) challenge parts of it; do not present as complete.
claims.uncertaintyText: Foundational statement from a peer-reviewed review, not a systematic review. It describes general biology and says nothing about any peptide product or treatment.

evidence.interpretation: Authors label this "classical concepts" and note newer findings (dendritic release, local synthesis) challenge parts of it; do not present as complete.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The review's own statement, with no citation attached; nothing behind it can be traced.

claims.claimText: Hevesi et al. (2025) state that neuropeptide degradation is enzymatic and occurs mostly in lysosomes.
claims.plainLanguageText: The body breaks neuropeptides down using enzymes.
claims.interpretationNotes: Specific to neuropeptides in the nervous system; do not generalise the "lysosomes" location to all peptide hormones.
claims.uncertaintyText: Foundational statement from a peer-reviewed review, not a systematic review. It describes general biology and says nothing about any peptide product or treatment.

evidence.interpretation: Specific to neuropeptides in the nervous system; do not generalise the "lysosomes" location to all peptide hormones.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The review's own statement, with no citation attached; nothing behind it can be traced.

claims.claimText: Ahmadi, Perez and Guardia (2025) describe specialised cells, such as pituitary lactotrophs and pancreatic beta cells, storing specific proteins in secretory granules and releasing them on stimulation.
claims.plainLanguageText: Some hormone-making cells keep their products packed in storage granules and release them when they receive the right signal.
claims.interpretationNotes: Statement is about secreted proteins generally (the next sentence lists hormones and neuropeptides among them). Examples are the source's own.
claims.uncertaintyText: Foundational statement from a peer-reviewed review, not a systematic review. It describes general biology and says nothing about any peptide product or treatment.

evidence.interpretation: Statement is about secreted proteins generally (the next sentence lists hormones and neuropeptides among them). Examples are the source's own.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The review's own statement, with no citation attached; nothing behind it can be traced.

claims.claimText: Wang (2014) describes host defence antimicrobial peptides as key components of the innate immune system in invertebrates and vertebrates.
claims.plainLanguageText: Some of the body's own peptides are part of its built-in defence against germs.
claims.interpretationNotes: Class description only. No claim about therapeutic use.
claims.uncertaintyText: Foundational statement from a peer-reviewed review, not a systematic review. It describes general biology and says nothing about any peptide product or treatment.

evidence.interpretation: Class description only. No claim about therapeutic use.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The review's own statement, with no citation attached; nothing behind it can be traced.

claims.claimText: Wang (2014) states that host defence peptides are usually made as precursor proteins, with the mature form released by protease processing.
claims.plainLanguageText: Defence peptides are also made as larger proteins first, then cut to release the working peptide.
claims.uncertaintyText: Foundational statement from a peer-reviewed review, not a systematic review. It describes general biology and says nothing about any peptide product or treatment.

evidence.primaryTraceNote: The review's own statement, with no citation attached; nothing behind it can be traced.

claims.claimText: Alford et al. (2020) give the example of human cathelicidin: a precursor protein (hCAP18) cleaved by proteases to generate the active peptide LL-37.
claims.plainLanguageText: One example: the body makes a protein called hCAP18, which is cut to produce an active defence peptide called LL-37.
claims.interpretationNotes: Illustrative endogenous example as given by the source; no therapeutic or product claims.
claims.uncertaintyText: Foundational statement from a peer-reviewed review, not a systematic review. It describes general biology and says nothing about any peptide product or treatment.

claims.claimText: Wang et al. (2022) state that endogenous GLP-1 is degraded by the enzyme dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) and rapidly inactivated.
claims.plainLanguageText: One example given in a review: the body's own GLP-1 is quickly broken down by an enzyme.
claims.interpretationNotes: Single illustrative example from a drug-development review; surrounding text concerns drugs and contains an error (see problems). Do not quote neighbouring sentences; do not generalise half-life figures.

claims.claimText: Wang (2014) states that what human antimicrobial peptides do can depend on biological context, peptide concentration, proteases and metabolic state.
claims.plainLanguageText: What one of the body's own peptides does can change with where it is, how much of it there is, and the state of the surrounding tissue.
claims.interpretationNotes: Stated for human AMPs only. Supports context-dependence; it does not itself say anything about safety of taking peptides.
claims.uncertaintyText: Foundational statement from a peer-reviewed review, not a systematic review. It describes general biology and says nothing about any peptide product or treatment.

evidence.interpretation: Stated for human AMPs only. Supports context-dependence; it does not itself say anything about safety of taking peptides.

claims.claimText: Hevesi et al. (2025) argue that the diversity of receptors, in location and over time, is the chief determinant of what any chemical messenger does.
claims.plainLanguageText: What a signalling molecule does depends mostly on which receptors are present, where, and when.
claims.interpretationNotes: Authors' interpretive statement in a review; attribute, do not present as settled law.

claims.claimText: Tse and Wong (2019) note that the same chemical molecules can be used in endocrine, paracrine, autocrine or synaptic signalling contexts.
claims.plainLanguageText: The same molecule can act as a long-distance hormone in one setting and a local signal in another.
claims.interpretationNotes: General statement; source does not name a peptide example in this sentence.

claims.claimText: Hiller-Sturmhöfel and Bartke (1998) describe feedback from target glands to the hypothalamus and pituitary keeping hormone-system activity within appropriate boundaries.
claims.plainLanguageText: The body uses feedback loops to keep hormone activity within a normal range.
claims.interpretationNotes: Describes hypothalamic-pituitary hormone cascades specifically, not all peptides. Does not by itself make a safety argument; editorial bridge to "the body makes it is not a safety argument" is SOURCE NEEDED.

notYetSupported.statement: Growth factors as a class of signals made by the body.
notYetSupported.why: No permissively licensed source retrieved describes them as a class.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: A CC BY-type review of growth factors, obtained and read.

notYetSupported.statement: That the body's own peptides are, as a general rule, short-lived and cleared by peptidases.
notYetSupported.why: The sources held describe enzymatic breakdown of neuropeptides and give one hormone example; none states the general rule.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: A permissively licensed review of peptide hormone clearance.

notYetSupported.statement: That 'the body makes it' is not, by itself, an argument about safety or efficacy.
notYetSupported.why: The facts it would rest on are sourced — effects depend on context, concentration and receptors, and hormone levels are held within range by feedback — but no source draws the conclusion, and this index does not draw it for them.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: A source that states the inference, or a scientific reviewer's approval of it as an editorial conclusion labelled as such.

resolution.note: Answered as Tides synthesis SYN-BODY-01, drawn from claims END-10 to END-13. No external source states the conclusion, so it is recorded as a synthesis that names the claims it rests on, not as a sourced fact.
